chunks: I2C ACK and NACK. The question: Explain NACK/ACK.
After every byte on an I2C bus, there is one extra clock tick, the ninth. On it, the receiver of the byte answers. If it accepted the byte, it pulls the data wire low.
That is an ACK. If it does nothing, the wire stays high, which is a NACK. A NACK is not a message anyone sends. It is silence, and it is not always an error.
Think of a teacher taking roll. The teacher calls a name, and a raised hand means "here". No hand means nothing happened, but you can't tell why.
The student might be absent, might not have heard, or might be busy. I2C works the same way.
A raised hand is the receiver pulling the wire low, and silence is the wire's pull-up resistor (which lifts it whenever nobody pulls down) leaving it high.
Two bytes on the bus.

In the first byte (bits 1, 0, 1 shown), the target pulls SDA low on the ninth clock: the SDA-bus row dips low while the controller row shows it released (dashed) and the target row shows it driving low: ACK.
In the second byte nobody drives on the ninth clock, so the bus rises to the pull-up level: NACK. Then the controller issues STOP.
ACK: the receiver pulls the data wire low on the ninth clock, meaning "got it." NACK: the wire stays high on the ninth clock, meaning nobody confirmed.
Receiver: whichever chip just received the byte. It makes the reply. On a read, that is the controller.
Bus scan: sending each address and noting which chips ACK, to find what is on the bus.
ACK polling: repeatedly addressing a memory chip until it ACKs, which shows its internal write has finished.
A NACK after the address means no chip answered: wrong address, no power, or missing pull-ups. A NACK after a byte the controller wrote means the chip rejected it.
At the end of a read, the controller NACKs the last byte on purpose, so the chip lets go of the wire and a STOP can follow. A memory chip busy writing NACKs its address.
One poll takes about 11 clock ticks, 110 microseconds at 100 kilohertz, so a 5 milliseconds write is polled about 45 times. That is the whole idea.
"The ninth clock after every byte is the acknowledge. The receiver of the byte pulls SDA low for an ACK; if nobody pulls it, the pull-up leaves it high, which is a NACK.

A NACK after the address means no device answered; after a written data byte it means the target rejected it; and on a read the controller deliberately NACKs the last byte so the target lets go of SDA for the STOP.
EEPROMs use NACK on their address while busy, so you poll until it ACKs."
